I've long been skeptical about the business case for humanoid robots.  I definitely see the advantage in deploying them in work environments already set up for people.  But I would expect a more efficient solution would be to build robotic warehouses deigned from the ground up for specialized, non-humanoid and presumably much simpler and less expensive robots.

It just seems to me that for almost any given specific application, you could design a much better form factor than one mimicking human beings.  But apparently a lot of wealthy investors think I'm wrong about that.  I've been wrong about a lot of things.

The robot dogs have always been interesting to me as mechanical pack animals.  I believe this was the original DoD application that gave Boston Dynamics its start.

I don't trust the FSD of my Tesla. But I could consider buying an Optimus to drive instead!

/S

comments.author: @Mirus-i
comments.text:
The history of Warfare reveals that when a new technology or strategy is developed that can be applied to the battle field, it is not long before that technology or strategy is deployed to conquer others that have not obtained the same capabilities.  

Recent major large scale wars, first and second Gulf War and Russian/Ukraine revealed that major large scale war technologies, tactics and strategies have peaked.  First and second Gulf War with Iraq revealed how superior weapons, numbers and tactics can quickly vanquish an entrenched Army.  Russian/Ukraine reveals that conventional warfare between two equally equipped forces results in a stalemate.

What is still effective is guerrilla warfare, which showed its effectiveness in Afghanistan.  And when used in a region of rough terrain and large land mass, a conventional Army that has advanced weapons and numbers will still have a difficult time uprooting the opposition.  However, Gaza has shown that Guerrilla tactics used within a limited land mass is no longer effective against a well equipped Army utilizing today’s moderately advanced weapons and surveillance/reconnaissance technologies.

I expect that the robotics advancements will reveal that Guerrilla tactics will not have the same effective strategy it once had where the ability of a smaller fighting force with basic modern weapons can play a long game to demoralize the invader via long term attrition of Human Resources. Not saying I like Guerrilla warfare.  But it has its place in history and played a major part in the American revolution.

With new advanced robotics that are insect, bird, dog, human, tank, plane and ship sized an Army can drastically limit the loss of humans in the process to root out opposition.  The main loss is monetary.  As long as money, manufacturing, supply lines and sentiment can be maintained by the invader/oppressor the smaller guerrilla force will not be able to wield the exhaustion tactics that have worked so well for thousands of years. 

The loss of effective Guerrilla warfare tactics, barring a Skynet scenario, is what concerns me the most in the short term. Although as mentioned in my first statement, in warfare, once a new technology is developed, it is not long before it is put to use.
